response_text:
FIFO scheduling is a first-in-first-out algorithm that processes jobs based on their arrival order. It ensures that the oldest job in the queue is executed immediately, guaranteeing fair treatment for all arriving processes regardless of their relative speed. This simple rule creates a predictable timeline where the earliest job always gets the first opportunity to run.

The core operation involves maintaining a queue where the head of the line holds the newest job. When a process arrives, it is added to the front of this queue, and the oldest job is removed and executed next. This structure prevents any single job from dominating the system by ensuring no one blocks others indefinitely.

A practical example involves a server managing a batch of incoming web requests. If a new client connects at 10:00 AM, the system immediately serves that request before processing the one arriving at 10:01 AM. This ensures that the most urgent or earliest requests are handled efficiently without waiting for later arrivals.

The primary advantage of FIFO is its simplicity and fairness. It treats all processes equally by prioritizing those who arrived first, preventing any single process from monopolizing resources. This makes it ideal for time-sensitive applications where fairness is more important than speed.

Head-of-line blocking occurs when a process waits indefinitely because the queue is full. Under FIFO, this is impossible since the oldest job is always processed first, so no one can block others. This eliminates the risk of starvation or deadlock that often plagues other scheduling methods.

Compared to other policies like Round Robin, FIFO offers better performance for time-critical tasks. While Round Robin gives each process a turn, FIFO ensures that the earliest job is always served first, reducing overall system latency. FIFO scheduling is a first-in-first-out algorithm that processes jobs based on their arrival order. It ensures that the oldest job in the queue is executed immediately, guaranteeing fair treatment for all arriving processes regardless of their relative timing. This simple rule creates a predictable and stable system where the earliest entry is always served first.

The core operation involves maintaining a queue where the head of the line holds the most recent job. When a process arrives, it is added to the front of this queue, and the oldest job is removed and executed next. This structure prevents any process from waiting indefinitely for a slot, ensuring that the system remains efficient and responsive.

A practical example involves a server managing multiple online applications. If a new client requests a resource, the oldest application is served first, while the newest one waits until the oldest one finishes. This behavior prevents the newest client from blocking the older one, which is crucial for maintaining system stability.

The primary advantage of FIFO is its simplicity and fairness. It treats all processes equally by prioritizing those that have arrived earliest, ensuring no single process dominates the system. This approach is ideal for real-time systems where consistent response times are critical.

Head-of-line blocking occurs when a process arrives after others have already been served, causing the queue to grow and delay subsequent arrivals. This can lead to significant delays for the newest process, especially in systems with limited resources.

Compared to other policies, FIFO is often preferred for its simplicity and predictable behavior. Unlike round-robin, which alternates between processes, FIFO does not change the order of arrival. It is particularly effective in environments where process priority is not the primary concern.
